voice_name: Daniel (ElevenLabs premade, neutral broadcaster; not an imitation of the author)

shots.text: A patient arrives with four records from three cities, in two languages. The pharmacy record says: allergic to sulfonamides. The newest letter, in Spanish, says: no known drug allergies.
This is for the receiving clinician: what is supported, what conflicts, what is missing.
Clocked Protect screens the records for names and ID numbers first. The conflict leads the page, quoted from both records, never resolved for you.

Clocked Extract copies each medication line word for word, from every record. Physician-signed rules set every label; no model decides one. Warfarin: in three records, missing from the newest. Bisoprolol: two point five milligrams, then five.

Clocked Fill drafts one sentence per discrepancy, and Clocked Verify checks each one against the original records. This allergy draft was removed: a sentence holding two disagreeing records reads as contradicted. So the rules rebuilt it from both exact quotes, and Verify checked each quote alone.
It also stays quiet. Metformin, written four ways in shorthand and Spanish: same dose, no flag. Before this normalisation, medication labels were 54 of 100.
Clocked Compare, run separately on the raw records, independently flagged 25 of the 39 conflicts the rules found.
Verify cannot prove that something is missing, so absences are established by comparing records, and labelled that way. No allergy in any record means unknown, not none.
On twenty synthetic patients: 100 of 100 medication labels, 5 of 5 allergy conflicts, all 70 discrepancies named in the handoff, where Fill and Verify alone reached 55. No invented medicines.
